newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels extend advance in Zaire, capture new town.
newsitem.headline: Rebels extend advance in Zaire, capture new town.

text.p: Rebels have captured the east Zaire town of Shabunda and are advancing towards Kindu, one of the springboards for the counter-offensive the army launched last month, church sources and aid workers said on Thursday.

The rebels, who have frustrated the army offensive by opening up new fronts, were advancing in large numbers towards Kindu, with its army base and airport around 200 km (125 miles) to the west, the sources added from the region.
The sources said that Shabunda fell on Wednesday.
Kindu is on the Lualaba river which flows north into the might Zaire River, which in turn flows through the strategic town of Kisangani on its way west to the Atlantic Ocean.
Up to 40,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees fled west into the forest earlier after reports that the Tutsi-led rebels, who launched their revolt in October, had taken nearby Katshunga.
One source said soldiers from Zaire's demoralised army fled through Shabunda on Tuesday and that local people gathered in a church and welcomed the arrival of the rebels.
Further north, on the road from the rebel-held east to Kisangani, relief workers spoke of a movement of people from Amisi refugee camp but had no details on the reason.

Amisi is about 280 km (170 miles) from Kisangani, headquarters of the counter offensive the army launched on January 20. Hardline Hutu fighters blamed for the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda were last reported there.
Aid workers said that further down the road all was calm at Tingi Tingi camp, where over 100,000 refugees are struggling with disease and lack of food.
Tingi Tingi is on the outskirts of Lubutu.
Zairean defence officials had no immediate comment on the details of the reports but denied suggestions by rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Wednesday that his forces were near Lubutu.
A senior Zairean Defence Ministry official said on Wednesday the army was rushing men and weapons to defend Lubutu and Moba, on a new front in the mineral-rich province of Shaba.
But the rebels say their thrusts on several fronts have stopped the counter-offensive in its tracks and have given President Mobutu Sese Seko until February 21 to stand down.

"We have built a motivated and dedicated army ready to liberate this country from 31 years of looting, plunder and destruction by Mobutu and his cronies," Kabila told reporters at his Goma headquarters in the east on Wednesday.

In Goma, some 5,000 newly-trained rebel troops paraded in the streets on Thursday singing battle songs praising Kabila and denouncing Mobutu as rebel officers said frontline units were advancing into mercenary-held territory in the north east.

Rebel officers said frontline units were about to enter the northeastern town of Isiro where some of the 300 foreign mercenaries hired by Kinshasa to crush the revolt are based. The units were closing in on mercenaries in Isiro, they added.
"The fall of Isiro is a matter of hours," a senior rebel commander told Reuters. Isiro is about 520 km (325 miles) northwest of Goma, which fell to the rebels in early November.

The rebel claims could not be independently confirmed but while Kabila says they are fighting alone, the United States has joined a growing chorus of international concern about the role played by Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi in the conflict.
"The United States appeals again to the neighbours of Zaire to stay out of Zaire, to not involve themselves in the fighting," a State Department spokesman said in Washington.

Israel on Thursday joined the growing list of Zaire's friends denying that they were helping the Kinshasa government by training or fighting alongside the army. Togo and Egypt have already made such denials.

Mobutu, said by aides to be returning home after fresh tests in Europe following cancer surgery in August, spent Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday in Morocco, which sent troops to help him crush rebellions in Shaba in the 1970s.
